Today is 2026-10-23.

WHO I AM AND WHAT I NEED
I am a researcher in an evidence-synthesis group preparing a submission to a workshop on the science of science and health policy. My subject is sugar-sweetened beverages, obesity and type 2 diabetes (central claim: sugar-sweetened beverage consumption increases the risk of type 2 diabetes). I need two things on one HTML page: a deep analytical report I will use internally, and a full research article I can revise and submit. Reviewers will check every number and every reference, so I would rather see a null result or "not measured" than a plausible figure with no origin. Describe only analyses you actually performed.

RESEARCH QUESTIONS (fixed; answer each with measured values or an explicit, grounded "cannot be measured")
RQ1 Attention: how has sugar-sweetened beverages, obesity and type 2 diabetes (central claim: sugar-sweetened beverage consumption increases the risk of type 2 diabetes) moved in the research literature (papers per year) and in the news (articles per month) over a stated window, and do the two move together? Quantify the change in each and the relation between them.
RQ2 Evidence: what do the clinical and health literatures say about the central claim? Give the strongest effect sizes with their populations and sources, the balance of supporting versus contradicting documents weighted by study tier, the direction of risk-factor claims where such a tally exists, and where the claim is contested.
RQ3 Geography: where is the subject studied (first-author affiliation), where is it published (journal country), where is it reported (country an article is about) and where is it patented (assignee country)? Show at least one country-level world map; keep the four lanes apart and never add them; quantify the mismatch between where it is studied and where it is reported; place India and at least three comparator countries on each lane.
RQ4 Trajectory: what is the three-year projection of at least one measured series, as observed points plus a central path with lower and upper bounds? State the method, the baseline it was chosen against, the backtest error against a no-change baseline, the last observed period and the gap to today, and what the series measures and does not measure. A projection from memory must be labelled estimate.
RQ5 Synthesis: taking the research literature, the health evidence, the news record and patents together, what is the one argument the data supports, and what does it change for a reader deciding what to study or fund next?

WHAT THE PAGE MUST CONTAIN (each item is checked)
A. Verdict, first: the answer to RQ5 in one or two sentences; the decision it supports; confidence (high, medium or low) with the reason; what would change it. At most 150 words, every number tagged.
B. Analytical report: one section per research question, every number tagged, measured separated from interpretation, with charts covering at least five of these seven dimensions: time; geography; comparison; composition (stance, orientation or study-tier shares); forecast; evidence magnitude (effect sizes or tiers); and source mix (research literature vs health literature vs news vs patents). Each chart has a title, unit, window, source and a one-sentence reading, backs a sentence in the text, and no two charts show the same quantity. The newest incomplete period is marked, never plotted as a collapse. At least two sentences connect measurements from two different sources into one argument.
C. Research article, inside <article id="research-article">, with these seven sections in this order as headings: Abstract (150 to 300 words), Introduction, Data and methods, Results, Discussion, Limitations, References. At least 2,000 words in total. Data and methods names every data source, query, phrase, lane, window and matching rule you used, and nothing you did not do. Results contain only findings that trace to your data (tagged) or to a cited reference. Discussion ties results to the literature with resolvable identifiers. Limitations are specific (data end date and gap to today, lane, coverage, title matching, censoring, patent publication lag) and say what would change the conclusions. Cite in the text as [r1], [r2] ... and list every cited entry under References with title, venue, year and a resolvable DOI or URL.
D. Drill-down: the next layer under each headline number (subcategories, countries, the key documents) with identifiers, and three to eight follow-up questions, each paired with the exact query that would answer it (a tool call with its arguments if you have a tool; otherwise the query in words).
E. Exports: at least three CSV tables (the yearly and monthly series; the country tables by lane; the key documents with identifiers, tiers and verbatim quotes), each with source, window, unit, coverage flag and export date, each named in the text, nulls as empty cells.
F. Method and limits placed beside the numbers they bound: the end date of the newest data and the gap to today; what each count is and is not; lanes; coverage; censoring; patent publication lag; thin evidence; what would close each gap.
G. References: up to 15 counted, each tied to a claim, quotes verbatim from the source.

RULES ON SOURCES
- Every number in the visible text carries an inline source tag: [c1], [c2] ... for a data query you ran during this task (declared in the calls list with its arguments); [r1], [r2] ... for an entry in References; or (est.) for a figure from memory. An untagged number is treated as unsourced.
- A chart, map, table, forecast or article finding whose values have no source and are not labelled estimate is scored as invented, and one invented element caps the whole page.
- An honest estimate label is never penalised for being an estimate. An honest literature review that performs no new analysis and says so is acceptable; an analysis you did not perform, described as performed, is not.
- Counted at most: 10 charts, 6 exports, 15 references, 8 follow-up queries. Extras are ignored unless they are invented.

FORMAT
=== DELIVERABLE CONTRACT (identical for every respondent) ===
Return ONE self-contained HTML document inside a single ```html fenced block, and nothing outside it.
- Charts: Vega-Lite 5 loaded from cdn.jsdelivr.net exactly as
  <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/vega@5.30.0"></script>
  <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/vega-lite@5.21.0"></script>
  <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/vega-embed@6.26.0"></script>
  and rendered with vegaEmbed('#<chart id>', spec) into an element whose id equals the chart's manifest id,
  with the data inline in each spec ("data": {"values": [...]}); the only file a spec may load is the map file below.
- Maps: country-level choropleths using the GeoJSON served next to the report at the relative URL
  "world_india_official.geojson" (Vega-Lite data {"url": "world_india_official.geojson", "format": {"type": "json",
  "property": "features"}}; each feature has properties.iso3, properties.name and properties.id = ISO numeric;
  India is drawn with the official Survey of India outline). Join your values with a lookup transform on
  "properties.iso3". Do not use any other map file. In the manifest, map points are [country name or ISO alpha-3, value].
- Every number shown on the page carries a source tag: [c1] [c2] ... (a call you made, declared in the
  manifest), [r1] [r2] ... (an entry in References) or (est.) (an estimate from memory). A chart, map, table or
  forecast whose values have no source and are not labelled estimate is scored as invented.
- The page MUST contain <script type="application/json" id="report-manifest"> holding JSON with keys:
  "verdict": {"answer": "...", "decision": "...", "confidence": "high|medium|low - reason", "what_would_change": "..."},
  "charts": [ {"id", "kind": "line|bars|hbar|share|map|forecast", "title", "unit",
               "window": {"from": "YYYY-MM-DD", "to": "YYYY-MM-DD"}, "x": {"field": "period|year|label|country", "type": "temporal|ordinal|geo"},
               "series": [{"name", "source": "call:<feature>#<n> | ref:rN | estimate", "points": [[x, value], ...]}],
               "forecast": {"method": "...", "source": "call:<feature>#<n> | estimate", "horizon": "...",
                            "points": [[x, central, lower, upper], ...]}   (kind=forecast only),
               "caption", "supports": "the sentence on the page this chart backs, verbatim"} ],
  "exports": [ {"name": "file.csv", "source", "window": "from..to", "unit", "coverage": "full|partial|unknown", "csv": "header\nrow..."} ],
  "calls": [ {"id": "c1", "feature", "args", "used_for"} ... , {"id": "f1", "question", "feature", "args"} ... ],
  "references": [ {"id": "r1", "title", "venue", "year", "doi_or_url"} ]
  Every chart drawn on the page appears in the manifest with the same values; the visible page and the
  manifest must agree. "calls" may be [] if you ran no data queries. Follow-up entries (f1..) give a next
  question and the query that would answer it: a tool feature and args if you have a tool, else the query in words.
- RESEARCHER TIER: the page also contains <article id="research-article"> with the sections Abstract,
  Introduction, Data and methods, Results, Discussion, Limitations, References (each as an <h2>).

Answer from your own knowledge only; do not run commands or browse. You may include charts, maps, tables and projections from your knowledge, with each series' source given as a named published source (ref:rN) or as estimate. Do not run any commands or tools.
